caution: Comparing risks measured on different bases is the easiest way to mislead yourself with numbers. So the chart below puts everything on ONE basis: the chance in a single year. Food risks are per-serving figures multiplied by an assumed eating frequency, which is stated on the chart; the anchors are published per-year figures. That makes them genuinely comparable, unlike a per-serving risk set beside a lifetime risk.

anchors.label: Getting food poisoning from any cause
anchors.note: CDC estimates roughly 1 in 6 Americans - about 48 million people - get a foodborne illness each year, from all causes combined.

annualisation: Food figures assume two servings a week, or 104 servings a year, of that specific food. That is an assumption we chose, not a measurement - if you eat a food far more or less often than that, scale accordingly. The arithmetic is a simple multiplication of the per-serving estimate, which is accurate enough at these small probabilities.
one_off_note: Some familiar odds are per single event rather than per year - a Powerball ticket is 1 in 292,200,000, a royal flush 1 in 649,740, ten heads in a row 1 in 1,024. They are left off the chart deliberately, because putting a per-event number on a per-year axis is exactly the error this section is trying to avoid.
